Photoreal 8K product photography of a single object on a flat neutral mid-grey seamless background. Museum artifact documentation lighting: broad soft even illumination from above and both sides, no directional shadows, no hot specular hits, no atmosphere, no vignette. The object is the only subject — no hands, no props, no set, no environment. Photographed straight down from directly above, the sheet filling the frame, corners curling slightly off the surface.

THE OBJECT — one small single leaf of hand-drawn paper, a late-fifteenth-century Spanish horoscope figure, roughly 20 by 28 centimeters, drawn freehand by a working astrologer with a cut quill.

THE HANDWRITING — CRITICAL. Every mark on this page was made by a quill pen dipped in iron gall ink five hundred years ago, and it must look it. Nothing on this sheet is printed, typeset, or evenly inked.
Quill behaviour: the stroke swells thick and dark on every downstroke and thins to a fine hairline on every upstroke and connecting stroke, the width changing continuously within single letters. Ink pools and darkens where the nib paused, at the start of a stroke and at the foot of each descender. Small ink blots and spatter where the pen was set down hard.
Dipping rhythm: each dip starts dark and heavy, then the ink runs progressively drier across the next several words until the stroke breaks up into a scratchy dry-nib skip, and then the next dip goes dark again. This cycle repeats visibly all down the page, so the ink density varies from word to word and no two lines are the same weight.
Cursive, not print: joined-up secretary-hand cursive with a rightward slant, ascenders and descenders tangling between lines, letter shapes irregular and no two instances of the same letter identical, the baseline wandering slightly, spacing uneven, the ends of lines cramping as they run out of room.
Age in the ink: the iron gall has oxidised from black to warm rust-brown, unevenly — some strokes still dark brown, others faded to pale tan, several words almost lost where the ink went thin. The ink has bled slightly into the paper fibre so edges are soft and feathered rather than crisp. In two or three places the ink has bitten into the sheet and browned the paper around the stroke.
Legible but aged — the words can be read, but they read as five-hundred-year-old handwriting, not as clean modern lettering.

THE CHART IS SQUARE, NOT ROUND. LOCATION comes from <<<image_1>>> — the Huei Tzompantli of Tenochtitlan, 1520. The skull rack fills the
frame behind the soldiers exactly as in the reference: weathered timber uprights, horizontal
crossbeams threaded through hundreds of human skulls in dense ordered grids stacked many courses
high, timber tops projecting above the topmost row against the flat grey sky, tiered stone courses
below carrying further rows of skulls facing outward, a low rough stone base, and the cylindrical
skull tower at the right edge. Pale cracked limestone paving runs along its base.

THE SHOT — a single file of Spanish conquistadors marches across the frame from RIGHT to LEFT in
clean side profile, along the paving in front of the rack. Camera square-on to their line of march
at eye level. Every man's body faces LEFT and every man's head faces LEFT down the line of march.
They move across the lens, not toward it and not away from it. Roughly twelve men, spaced unevenly,
the nearest filling the lower third of frame and the rest smaller down the line to the left. All
mid-stride, weight dropped into the leading foot, out of step with one another.
They are dwarfed by the rack — it stands as tall as four men stacked head to toe and fills the upper
two thirds of frame while the men occupy only the lower third.

NOBODY LOOKS AT THE WALL. Every head faces straight forward along the line of march, chins level,
eyes front. Not one man turns his head, tilts his chin, glances back or looks up. They walk past it.

SPEARS — roughly one man in three carries a Spanish spear held upright, butt near the ground, shaft
rising vertically past his shoulder. Long plain weathered wooden shafts with simple leaf-shaped steel
heads, rising against the rack behind, each leaning at a slightly different angle, never parallel.

An orthographic prop reference sheet for a Spanish military crossbow
(ballesta) of around 1500, rendered as a film prop department turnaround on a
flat warm-grey backdrop, with a bolt loaded and in place.

Layout: three views of the weapon lying horizontally, stacked one above
another across a wide landscape sheet — top-down plan, left side profile, and
underside — each running the full width from left to right, straight-on with
no perspective distortion. The stirrup end sits at the left. To the right,
four circular detail insets at larger scale: the hemp binding where the prod
meets the tiller, the rotating nut and trigger lever, the loaded bolt seated
against the string, and the bolt head.

The weapon: about 90 centimetres from stirrup to butt end, heavy and compact.

The prod: a single leaf of forged spring steel spanning roughly 70
centimetres, thick and narrow at the centre and tapering toward each tip,
slightly recurved, mounted transversely through the front of the tiller. Dark
grey-brown steel with a matte oiled finish, no polish, faint hammer texture.

The binding, critical: the prod passes through a mortice cut LOW in the front
of the tiller, well below the upper surface. It is held entirely by cord —
many tight turns of coarse hemp wrapped around the underside and both sides
of the tiller and over the prod, dozens of visible windings packed close
together, darkened with oil and grime, with small hardwood wedges driven in
to lock it. The binding stays BELOW the level of the bolt groove and does not
cross, cover or pass over the top face of the tiller at any point. The upper
surface of the tiller remains completely clear and unobstructed from the nut
forward past the muzzle, so the bolt has an open path. No bolts, no screws,
no metal brackets.

The tiller: a straight stock of dark walnut, roughly rectangular in section,
deepest at the front and tapering toward a plain squared butt end. It is
STRAIGHT along its whole length with NO shoulder stock, NO buttplate and NO
drop at the rear — the butt is a simple tapered block of wood with no shaping
of any kind. A shallow groove runs down the centre of the upper face from nut
to muzzle for the bolt to sit in. The wood is oiled, scuffed, and darkened
where hands have gripped it, with a few small inlaid pieces of pale bone set
into the sides as sparse decoration.

The lock: a rotating nut of stag antler set into a socket across the tiller,
pale cream-brown against the dark wood, its two fingers holding the drawn
bowstring, with a thin retaining cord wound around the socket. Beneath the
tiller, a long slender iron trigger lever running back along the underside,
plain and undecorated, ending in a simple curved tip — not a modern trigger
and no trigger guard.

The string: hemp cord, thick and heavily whipped with thread at the centre
serving, drawn back and locked in the nut so the prod is under visible
tension and bent into a shallow arc.

The stirrup: a stout D-shaped iron loop riveted to the front end of the
tiller and hanging DOWNWARD below it, wide enough for a boot toe, scuffed to
bright metal on its lower curve. It sits entirely beneath the tiller and does
not rise above the bolt groove or cross the bolt's path.

Fittings: a transverse iron lug projecting from each side of the tiller
behind the nut for a spanning device to hook onto. A small iron suspension
ring at the butt end.

The bolt, loaded in place: a short thick shaft of hardwood about 30
centimetres long, seated in the groove on the upper face of the tiller with
its rear end resting against the drawn string, ready to shoot. The shaft is
barrel-tapered, thickest just behind the head and narrowing toward the rear.
Two vanes only, cut from thin stiff leather, low and narrow, set opposite one
another and bound to the shaft with fine thread and glue. The head is a
square-section pyramidal iron point, socketed onto the shaft, dark and
unpolished with a sharp tip. The bolt lies in a clear unobstructed groove
with nothing crossing above or in front of it along its full length.

Condition: campaign-used and serviceable. Steel dark and lightly rusted at
the prod tips, wood scuffed, hemp binding frayed at the outer turns, stirrup
worn bright, everything sound and correctly assembled. Nothing shines.

Rendering: flat even studio lighting, minimal shadow, high detail, accurate
material separation between forged steel, dark oiled walnut, coarse hemp
cord, pale antler, and stiff leather. Archaeological illustration precision
with the neutral clarity of a production reference photo. No hands, no
figure, no environment, no text.

An orthographic prop reference sheet for a Spanish military crossbow
(ballesta) of around 1500, rendered as a film prop department turnaround on a
flat warm-grey backdrop, with a bolt loaded and in place.

FRAMING, critical: exactly TWO views of the weapon, and no more. Each shows
the ENTIRE weapon from the stirrup at one end to the butt at the other,
complete and uncropped, nothing running off the edge of the sheet and nothing
cut off. Each view is scaled down as far as necessary to fit the full length
within the frame, with a clear margin of empty backdrop at both ends and
above and below. It is better for the weapon to appear small on the sheet
than for any part of it to be cropped. Both views are at the same scale as
one another and aligned on a common vertical centreline.

Layout: the two views lie horizontally, stacked one above the other in the
left two-thirds of a wide landscape sheet — TOP-DOWN PLAN above, LEFT SIDE
PROFILE below — each shown complete end to end, straight-on with no
perspective distortion. The stirrup end sits at the left in both. In the
right third, four circular detail insets at larger scale: the hemp binding
where the prod meets the tiller, the rotating nut and trigger lever, the
loaded bolt seated against the string, and the bolt head and flat rear end.

The weapon: about 90 centimetres from stirrup to butt end, heavy and compact.

The prod: a single leaf of forged spring steel spanning roughly 70
centimetres, thick and narrow at the centre and tapering toward each tip,
slightly recurved, mounted transversely through the front of the tiller. Dark
grey-brown steel with a matte oiled finish, no polish, faint hammer texture.
In the top-down view the prod is seen across its full span, both tips visible
and well inside the frame.

The binding, critical: the prod passes through a mortice cut LOW in the front
of the tiller, well below the upper surface. It is held entirely by cord —
many tight turns of coarse hemp wrapped around the underside and both sides
of the tiller and over the prod, dozens of visible windings packed close
together, darkened with oil and grime, with small hardwood wedges driven in
to lock it. The binding stays BELOW the level of the bolt groove and does not
cross, cover or pass over the top face of the tiller at any point. The upper
surface of the tiller remains completely clear and unobstructed from the nut
forward past the muzzle, so the bolt has an open path. No bolts, no screws,
no metal brackets.

The tiller: a straight stock of dark walnut, roughly rectangular in section,
deepest at the front and tapering toward a plain squared butt end. It is
STRAIGHT along its whole length with NO shoulder stock, NO buttplate and NO
drop at the rear — the butt is a simple tapered block of wood with no shaping
of any kind. A shallow groove runs down the centre of the upper face from nut
to muzzle for the bolt to sit in. The wood is oiled, scuffed, and darkened
where hands have gripped it, with a few small inlaid pieces of pale bone set
into the sides as sparse decoration.

The lock: a rotating nut of stag antler set into a socket across the tiller,
pale cream-brown against the dark wood, its two fingers holding the drawn
bowstring, with a thin retaining cord wound around the socket. Beneath the
tiller, a long slender iron trigger lever running back along the underside,
plain and undecorated, ending in a simple curved tip — not a modern trigger
and no trigger guard. The trigger lever is clearly visible in the side
profile view.

The string: hemp cord, thick and heavily whipped with thread at the centre
serving, drawn back and locked in the nut so the prod is under visible
tension and bent into a shallow arc.

The stirrup: a stout D-shaped iron loop riveted to the front end of the
tiller and hanging DOWNWARD below it, wide enough for a boot toe, scuffed to
bright metal on its lower curve. It sits entirely beneath the tiller and does
not rise above the bolt groove or cross the bolt's path. It is fully visible
and uncropped in the side profile view.

Fittings: a transverse iron lug projecting from each side of the tiller
behind the nut for a spanning device to hook onto. A small iron suspension
ring at the butt end.

THE BOLT, loaded in place, seated in the groove on the upper face of the
tiller with its rear end resting flat against the drawn string, ready to
shoot. It is shown complete, head to rear end, in both views.

Proportions, critical: the bolt is SLIM. The shaft is 30 centimetres long and
only 12 millimetres across at its widest — roughly twenty-five times longer
than it is thick. It is short but slender, and must NOT read as fat, stubby,
pudgy, club-like, cigar-shaped or bulging.

The shaft: turned from straight-grained ash in pale honey-brown wood, round
in section. It is thickest just behind the head and tapers evenly and gently
along its entire length down to 9 millimetres at the rear — a single straight
taper from front to back, with NO swelling in the middle and NO barrel shape.
The rear end is cut FLAT and square across, with no nock, no slot and no
notch of any kind — the bowstring pushes against a flat face.

The fletching: two vanes only, cut from thin stiff leather in dark brown, set
opposite one another on either side of the shaft, beginning about 4
centimetres from the rear end. Each vane is roughly 7 centimetres long and
only 12 millimetres high — low, narrow and lying close to the shaft, not tall
and not feather-shaped. Each is glued flat along its length and bound at both
ends with fine waxed thread.

The head: a socketed iron point 6 centimetres long, square in section,
tapering evenly to a needle-sharp pyramidal tip. The socket is the same
diameter as the shaft so there is no step, collar or flare where they meet.
Dark unpolished iron with visible hammer facets.

The bolt lies in a clear unobstructed groove with nothing crossing above or
in front of it along its full length.

Condition: campaign-used and serviceable. Steel dark and lightly rusted at

A narrow street in Tenochtitlan, Mexica capital, May 1520, seen at eye level from the middle of the street looking straight down its length. Heavy flat overcast, full cloud cover, soft omnidirectional daylight, no visible sun, no hard shadows anywhere, sky blown to featureless pale grey-white.

ARCHITECTURE
Single-story flat-roofed Mesoamerican houses press in on both sides, walls of stone rubble and adobe finished in thick lime stucco, hand-troweled and slightly uneven, weathered and stained near the ground. Most are bone white; a good number are painted — broad bands of deep red ochre at the base and around the doorways, panels of yellow ochre, dark turquoise-blue borders, black geometric step-fret and spiral motifs running as a frieze below the roofline. Paint is faded, sun-bleached and patchy, with the stucco showing through in places. Doorways are simple rectangular openings hung with plain cotton cloth curtains, no wooden doors. Low parapets run around every roof, roughly waist height. Wooden ladders lean against several walls. Potted plants, drying maguey fiber, stacked reed mats and clay water jars sit on the roofs. A shallow canal runs along one side of the street with a narrow stone walkway beside it and two empty dugout canoes drawn up and tied. The street surface is packed earth and worn flagstone, swept clean, wet in patches.

FAR BACKGROUND
At the end of the street, small in the distance and partly veiled in pale haze, <<<image_1>>> — the Great Temple precinct of Tenochtitlan rising above the rooftops. It is far away and reads as a silhouette of mass and stepped stairways, not as the subject of the shot. Everything nearer than it is sharp; the temple sits soft in atmospheric haze at three hundred meters.

THE PEOPLE
Both rooflines are lined shoulder to shoulder with Nahuatl-speaking Mexica people looking down into the street toward camera. Hundreds of faces, packed along every parapet as far down the street as the eye can follow, standing still. Nobody is shouting, nobody is moving. They are watching, and the expression on them is anger held in — set jaws, hard flat stares, lowered brows, arms folded or hands resting on the parapet.

Men wear the maxtlatl loincloth and a tilmatli cloak knotted over one shoulder, mostly undyed maguey and cotton in white, cream and pale tan, some in earth red or ochre, a few with woven border patterns. Women wear the huipil tunic over a wrapped cueitl skirt, white and cream with red, black and blue-green embroidered borders at neck and hem. Hair: men shoulder-length and blunt-cut with a straight fringe, some tied back; women in long braids wound up and tied at the crown or hanging loose. Most are barefoot; some men wear plain leather sandals. Simple jade, shell and obsidian ear ornaments and necklaces on some, nothing ostentatious.

Roughly one in five holds a weapon — a long obsidian-edged wooden spear held upright and vertical, butt resting on the roof, hand loose on the shaft. Not one weapon is raised or pointed. A few round shields lean against parapets. A handful of men wear quilted white cotton armor.

FACE VARIATION
Every person is a different individual, readable at a glance. Broad faces and narrow ones, aquiline and straight and broad noses, heavy brows and fine ones, full cheeks and gaunt ones. Ages from early twenties to elderly, with grey hair and deep lines on the older people. Builds from slight to heavy. Skin tones across the full range of warm brown. Scars, weathering, sun-lined faces. No two people look like the same person.

FRAMING AND OPTICS

No Spaniards, no Europeans, no horses, no European clothing, armor, helmets or steel anywhere in frame.
Every person in frame is a grown adult.
All spears are held vertical and grounded; none is raised, thrown or leveled.

A photorealistic wide photograph looking across the large interior courtyard of a

carriage sits back in the courtyard aimed squarely at the gate.

weathered original stucco. In the side ranges, several rooms stand open with their roof

Scattered signs of occupation: straw pallets under the colonnade, stacked shields, large

THE ROOM
Use the attached image as the reference for the architecture, materials and proportions — the same pale limestone walls in warm grey-cream plaster, the same painted stepped-fret banding as a wide frieze near the ceiling and a narrow double band at dado height in dark red and slate blue, the same heavy dark timber ceiling beams in close parallel courses, the same large pale limestone floor slabs with visible joints, the same recessed rectangular wall niches, the same low stone dais of two broad steps against the far wall with fret banding along its riser. Same scale, same restraint — a fine room, plain and severe.

CHANGES FROM THE REFERENCE
No doorway, no balcony opening, no view outside. The left wall is solid and unbroken, carrying the same plaster and painted banding across its full width. No chair, no throne, no seat of any kind. The dais is bare stone with woven reed mats laid across it.

THE GOLD BARS
Roughly two hundred crude hand-cast ingots — uneven edges, pitted and slightly misshapen from casting in open sand moulds, warm yellow, the cast surface rough but rubbed to a low sheen on the upper faces and along the edges where they have been handled and stacked. No stamps, no markings, no coins anywhere. Stacked in low tiers across the dais steps and along the base of the far wall, some stacks squared, others loose and leaning, a few bars fallen flat on the floor slabs where they slid off a pile. More gathered on reed mats spread across the floor.

AZTEC AND MIXTEC GOLDWORK
Lost-wax cast pieces, each one slightly different from its neighbours because each mould was broken to release it — no two identical. Warm gold that varies piece to piece from deep yellow to a coppery reddish cast, most of it burnished bright, some duller where the alloy shows through.
— Large cast pectorals worn on the chest, openwork, some in the form of feathered serpents with curling volutes and panaches, some as deity faces with rectangular openwork frames and small dangling bells along the lower edge.
— Ear spools and ear flares: broad hollow discs and flared tubes, some with fine drawn-wire filigree and granulation fused across the surface.
— Labrets: lip ornaments with a flat plate and a shaft, several with cast eagle and serpent heads.
— Cast bells in graduated sizes, hollow and pear-shaped with a slit mouth, strung in clusters.
— Necklaces of dozens of small hollow cast beads in the form of frogs, turtles and shells, each bead a fraction of an inch across.
— Thin hammered sheet-gold discs and perforated sheet ornaments, some crumpled at the edges, their curved surfaces catching the light in bright bands.
— Nose ornaments, finger rings, arm and leg bands.

JADE AND TURQUOISE
— Turquoise mosaic pieces: carved cedar wood cores completely covered in small tessellated turquoise tiles set in dark pine resin, with details picked out in red thorny oyster shell and white conch shell, and eyes inlaid with pyrite and shell. Include a double-headed serpent pectoral with an undulating body and a head at each end, and one or two mosaic masks. Surfaces finely fitted, slightly irregular, glossy where polished.
— Jade and greenstone: long multi-strand necklaces of polished round and tubular beads in mottled blue-green, apple green and grey-green, heaped in coils; large polished jade ear flares; small carved greenstone figures and beads; a carved jade mask.
— Gold pieces set with turquoise, jade-green stone, red shell and obsidian inlay.
— A few pieces in rock crystal, amethyst and obsidian, polished to a deep shine.

The room is full. Gold reads as soft heavy metal with a real burnish — polished enough to reflect, so curved and rounded surfaces carry bright travelling highlights and small pieces throw sharp specular points. Flat cast faces stay matte and porous by contrast, hammered surfaces show tool marks catching the light along their ridges, filigree and granulation glint as fine raised texture. Polished jade, turquoise and rock crystal pick up small hard highlights of their own. The mass of gold bounces a faint warm glow onto the pale plaster of the far wall and onto the underside of the dais step above it. Stones are polished but not faceted. Everything sits with real weight, the mats compressing under the stacks.

Photorealistic architectural rendering. Naturalistic color, restrained contrast, fine natural grain. No people, no figures, no modern objects, no text. Real metal specularity, but no bloom, no glow, no lens flare, no glitter effect, no treasure-cave lighting. Maximum resolution, 16:9.

THE OBJECT: a cacaxtli — a Mesoamerican porter's carrying frame from 1520 central Mexico, loaded with gold.

CONSTRUCTION: a light open pack frame built from rough-hewn wooden poles. Two vertical uprights about three feet long, with four or five horizontal crosspieces lashed between them at intervals with twisted maguey fiber cord, forming an open ladder-like rack. Two shorter poles angle back from the base to form a small shelf or platform at the bottom where the load rests. All joints are bound with cord wrapping, not nails or joinery. The wood is unfinished, pale tan, worn smooth and darkened where hands and loads have rubbed it.

THE TUMPLINE: a broad woven band of coarse fiber, about three inches wide at its center and tapering to cords at both ends, tied to the two lower corners of the frame. This is the mecapatl — the strap that goes across the porter's forehead so the load hangs from the head and neck. It should hang loose and visible in the standing views, its center band worn shiny and darkened from use.

THE LOAD: cloth-wrapped bundles lashed onto the frame with cord. The cloth is coarse undyed maguey fiber, oatmeal and tan, stained and travel-worn, tied off with knotted cord. The bundles are small and dense relative to the frame — heavy for their size — and sag the cord where they are lashed. In one bundle the cloth has split open at a corner, and two rough-cast gold bars are visible pushing through the gap: crude, uneven, hastily poured ingots with rounded lumpy surfaces and rough edges, dull and matte rather than polished, more like slag than treasure.

Stacked in low tiers across the dais steps and along the base of the far wall, some stacks squared, others loose and leaning, a few bars fallen flat on the floor slabs where they slid off a pile. More gathered on reed mats spread across the floor.

AZTEC AND MIXTEC GOLDWORK
Lost-wax cast pieces, each slightly different from its neighbours because each mould was broken to release it — no two identical. Warm gold varying piece to piece from deep yellow to a coppery reddish cast, some surfaces bright, others duller where the alloy shows through.
— Large cast pectorals worn on the chest, openwork, some as feathered serpents with curling volutes and panaches, some as deity faces in rectangular openwork frames with small dangling bells along the lower edge.
— Ear spools and ear flares: broad hollow discs and flared tubes, some with fine drawn-wire filigree and granulation fused across the surface.
— Labrets: lip ornaments with a flat plate and a shaft, several with cast eagle and serpent heads.
— Cast bells in graduated sizes, hollow and pear-shaped with a slit mouth, strung in clusters.
— Necklaces of dozens of small hollow cast beads in the form of frogs, turtles and shells, each bead a fraction of an inch across.
— Thin hammered sheet-gold discs and perforated sheet ornaments, some crumpled at the edges.
— Nose ornaments, finger rings, arm and leg bands.

JADE AND TURQUOISE
— Turquoise mosaic pieces: carved cedar wood cores completely covered in small tessellated turquoise tiles set in dark pine resin, details picked out in red thorny oyster shell and white conch shell, eyes inlaid with pyrite and shell. Include a double-headed serpent pectoral with an undulating body and a head at each end, and one or two mosaic masks. Finely fitted, slightly irregular, glossy where polished.
— Jade and greenstone: long multi-strand necklaces of polished round and tubular beads in mottled blue-green, apple green and grey-green, heaped in coils; large polished jade ear flares; small carved greenstone figures and beads; a carved jade mask.
— Gold pieces set with turquoise, jade-green stone, red shell and obsidian inlay.
— A few pieces in rock crystal, amethyst and obsidian, polished to a deep shine.

SPANISH GOLD
A small quantity only, in an open iron-banded wooden chest on the floor: rings, a plain gold cup, a few devotional pendants and crosses, loose worked fragments. Kept apart from the Aztec material.

DISTRIBUTION
The room is full. Gold and jewelry occupy most of the floor, the dais and the steps, heaped in shallow woven baskets and wide low ceramic bowls that overflow, spilling onto the reed mats and the bare stone around them. Necklaces spill over basket rims and pool on the floor. A small gold pot sits in each wall niche. Open swept limestone floor remains only in the near foreground toward camera.

MATERIALS AND FINISH
Gold reads as soft heavy metal — matte or lightly burnished, with broad dull highlights rather than mirror reflections. Cast surfaces rough and porous, hammered surfaces showing tool marks, filigree and granulation as fine raised texture. Stones polished but not faceted. Everything sits with real weight, the mats compressing under the stacks.

LIGHT
Firelight is the key. The brazier and the ocote torches throw warm restless orange light low across the floor and up the near faces of the gold stacks, raking hard across the ingots so the cast texture reads, and dying off fast into deep shadow in the corners and along the upper walls. Each flame throws its own pool and its own set of long shadows, so the gold is lit unevenly — some pieces catching a bright warm edge, others sunk in near darkness. Polished jade, turquoise and rock crystal pick up small sharp specular points from the flames. The hanging Spanish lamp throws a small steady pool of its own on the wall behind it. A faint cool ambient wash falls from a high vent off frame, just enough to keep the ceiling beams and the upper walls readable. Deep blacks with clean shadow detail. Warm, moody, underlit and rich — never bright, never flat.

CAMERA
Wide interior view at standing eye level, the room reading in full depth from the near floor to the far wall and dais. Neutral rectilinear lens, no distortion, deep focus with the whole room sharp.

STYLE
Photorealistic architectural rendering. Naturalistic color, restrained contrast, matte finish, fine natural grain, practical firelight only. No people, no figures, no coins, no chains, no candles, no modern objects, no text. Not glittering, no bloom, no lens flare, no treasure-cave lighting. Maximum resolution, 16:9.
